douse

DOWSS (rhymes with house) · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To douse is to drench something with liquid, put out a fire with water, or switch off a light.

A sudden downpour doused the bonfire before the fire department even arrived.

Example

As a prank, his roommates crept up while he was sleeping and doused him with a bucket of ice water.

Whether it's putting out a flame or soaking someone completely, douse always involves a sudden, thorough dose of liquid. Both senses share that same drenching, extinguishing action.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

extinguish: To extinguish a fire is to put it out completely, by any means — water, foam, or simply letting it burn down. Douse is narrower and wetter: you douse something by suddenly throwing liquid all over it, whether or not a fire is involved.

drench: To drench is to soak a person or thing through with liquid — a storm drenches a hiker. It says nothing about fire or purpose. Douse adds a sudden, deliberate throw of liquid, and it is the word you use for putting flames out.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

ignite: to set fire to; to start burning

kindle: to start a fire burning

Where it sits · how thoroughly something gets soaked — dampen → douse → flood

dampen vs. douse: To dampen something is to make it slightly wet, a much smaller amount of liquid than a full douse.

flood vs. douse: To flood something is to submerge it completely under water, an even more total soaking than a douse usually implies.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Douse is a very physical, hands-on word -- you douse an actual fire or an actual person with actual liquid. It's rarely used figuratively the way words like squelch or thwart often are.
